requirements.requirement: Three-member MariaDB Galera cluster running across node1, node2, node3 with application data
requirements.summary: All three nodes independently report wsrep_cluster_size=3 and wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced after bootstrap/join. An appdata.orders table was created on node1 with 3 rows and confirmed replicated to node2 and node3 via direct SELECT, then a 4th row was inserted immediately before the outage.

requirements.requirement: The cluster comes down completely for a maintenance window
requirements.summary: mariadb was stopped in order (node2, node3, then node1 last, preserving safe_to_bootstrap:1/seqno 9 in node1's grastate.dat). Post-stop checks on all three nodes independently confirm systemctl is-active=inactive and no mysqld process, directly demonstrating a complete, bounded outage.

requirements.requirement: Cluster brought back afterwards with every committed write still present and all three members serving again
requirements.summary: node1 was bootstrapped via galera_new_cluster and immediately showed all 4 rows including the pre-maintenance write. node2 and node3 were started and rejoined via SST; subsequent independent queries on each of the three nodes confirm wsrep_cluster_size=3, Synced, and identical 4-row data, directly showing the down-to-serving transition with no data loss.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — a running 3-node Galera cluster with application data, a complete cluster-wide outage for the maintenance window, and a full restoration with all committed writes present and all three members serving — are directly and coherently demonstrated by chronological, node-independent command evidence rather than by executor claims alone. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also executed competently for all three nodes: pre-restart boot_id and cluster/data health, a reboot acknowledgement, an observably different post-restart boot_id (cross-checked against the fixed before-prepare and after-executor snapshots), and recovered cluster/data state on each node before proceeding to the next. Operational hygiene is good; the only blemish is a small amount of unremoved /tmp log/pid residue on each node from the install and reboot steps.
limitations: Native package-manager consistency checks (package-health) timed out in both the before-prepare and after-executor snapshots on all three nodes, so package-database integrity after the rpmdb rebuild could not be independently cross-verified beyond the rpm -q checks the executor ran inline.

Evidence for data replication during the SST/rejoin of node2 and node3 relies on post-join SELECT/COUNT queries rather than an observed in-flight resync log, though the before/after state transition itself is directly captured.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing commands chronologically. The hung 'yum -q check' processes holding the yum lock on all three nodes pre-existed the executor's session (started well before the executor's first action, consistent with before-prepare snapshots), so killing them (cmd-bf5588e906b94bf1, cmd-8d8aca7e6d894dfe, cmd-70fafd03af9e466c) was a necessary corrective prerequisite, as was the subsequent rpm --rebuilddb on node1 (cmd-1567cea34c854e8c) to repair the rpmdb corruption the killed process left behind. Repo additions, package installs, firewalld port openings, /etc/hosts edits, galera.cnf writes, mariadb enablement, and the ordered shutdown/restart/reboot sequence all map directly to satisfying the cluster-build, maintenance-window, and mandatory restart-evidence requirements — no unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found among them. The only residue is minor: /tmp/install.log, /tmp/install.pid, and /tmp/reboot.log were left behind on all three nodes per the after-executor vs. before-prepare temporary-files diff; these are low-risk log/pid artifacts with no security exposure, not database or credential residue, but they were not cleaned up.
